name: iptables
description: The classic Linux firewall tool: chains of rules filtering packets by interface, address, port, and state. Superseded by nftables but still everywhere.

flags.description: List rules with counters, no DNS lookups.
Target: allow / silently drop / reject with notice.

examples.explanation: Lists the INPUT chain. Policy ACCEPT with explicit rules; --line-numbers gives you the numbers needed for -D/-I.
Allows HTTPS traffic. Rules apply immediately but vanish at reboot unless persisted (netfilter-persistent, iptables-save).
Inserts a block for one source IP at the top of the chain — the classic emergency ban.

about: iptables filters packets through chains (INPUT for the host, FORWARD for routed traffic, OUTPUT leaving). Rules match top-down; first match wins, so rule ORDER is the whole game. nftables (nft) replaces it with cleaner syntax and better performance; on modern kernels iptables commands are often translated to nftables behind the scenes.
useCases: Precise firewall control on older systems.
mistakes: Locking yourself out by setting INPUT policy DROP before allowing SSH.
Forgetting the ESTABLISHED rule and breaking all return traffic.
Expecting rules to persist across reboots without iptables-save.
warnings: iptables rules are live immediately — a bad INSERT on a remote server can cut your session. Always keep an out-of-band console (cloud provider console) available when editing firewalls remotely.
distroNotes: iptables-nft on modern distros translates to nftables. Pure nftables systems may lack iptables entirely.
